questions.question: Calculate the kinetic energy of the 1 000 kg car at 20 m/s, naming the order of operations that protects against the commonest error.
questions.expected_answer: Square the velocity first, as its own line: v² = 400. Then E_k = ½ × 1 000 × 400 = 500 × 400 = 200 000 J (200 kJ). The separate squaring line prevents the forgotten-square error, which would give ½ × 1 000 × 20 = 10 000 J — twenty times too small. Unit check: kg·m²/s² = J.

questions.question: Explain why kinetic energy is a scalar that can never be negative, even though velocity is a vector.
questions.expected_answer: The velocity enters the formula squared, and squaring erases the sign/direction: +20 and −20 both square to 400, so eastbound and westbound cars carry identical energy. Physically, energy measures capacity to do work, and damage has no compass. Since mass is positive and v² ≥ 0, E_k ≥ 0, with zero (rest) as the floor — no direction is ever attached to an energy answer.

questions.question: In your own words, explain the road-safety meaning of the square in ½mv², using the 20 m/s versus 40 m/s comparison.
questions.expected_answer: Doubling speed from 20 to 40 m/s raises the energy from 200 000 J to 800 000 J — four times, because 2² = 4 (tripling gives nine times). All that energy must be dissipated to stop: with the same braking force, roughly four times the braking distance; in a crash, four times the destruction to absorb. Energy also piles up top-heavily: 100→120 km/h adds more energy than 0→60 km/h. Speed limits reflect this quadratic arithmetic.
